MAKEUP TIME FOR PERSONAL OBLIGATIONS (LAB. CODE § 513) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this Makeup Time information sheet to describe what California law says about "makeup work time" — an arrangement under which a nonexempt employee such as Jordan Lee who loses work time because of a personal obligation may, on the employee's own signed written request and with the employer's approval, work those lost hours at another time in the same workweek without the added hours being counted toward daily overtime, within limits fixed by statute. This document describes the governing statute (Labor Code section 513), the parallel provision of the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders, the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published enforcement positions, and how makeup time differs from the separate "compensating time off" arrangement in Labor Code section 204.3. It describes the law; it does not create, request, approve, or deny any makeup-time arrangement.

THE DAILY OVERTIME RULE THAT MAKEUP TIME MODIFIES
California's overtime statute, Labor Code section 510(a), provides that eight hours of labor constitutes a day's work, and that work in excess of eight hours in one workday, work in excess of 40 hours in a workweek, and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in a workweek are compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay, with work beyond 12 hours in a day (and beyond eight hours on a seventh day) compensated at no less than twice the regular rate. Because California imposes overtime on a daily as well as a weekly basis, an employee who shifts hours from one day to another within the same week — for example, leaving three hours early on Tuesday and working three extra hours on Thursday — would ordinarily trigger daily overtime on the longer day even though the weekly total is unchanged. The makeup-time provision described in the following clauses is a statutory exception to that daily-overtime consequence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Eight hours of labor constitutes a day’s work. Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee. Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 510(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the general daily and weekly overtime thresholds in Labor Code section 510(a). Section 510(a) itself states that its requirements do not apply to overtime paid to an employee working under an alternative workweek schedule adopted under Labor Code section 511, under a collective bargaining agreement under section 514, or under section 554; those alternative-workweek arrangements are addressed in this project's separate Alternative Workweek Schedule Election information sheet and are not repeated here. The illustrative Tuesday/Thursday example in the body is this document's own arithmetic illustration of how a daily-overtime standard operates, not a quotation from, or an example in, any cited source.

LABOR CODE SECTION 513: THE MAKEUP-TIME EXCEPTION AND ITS 11-HOUR AND 40-HOUR LIMITS
Labor Code section 513, added in 1999 and effective January 1, 2000, provides that if an employer approves a written request of an employee to make up work time that is or would be lost as a result of a personal obligation of the employee, the hours of that makeup work time — if performed in the same workweek in which the work time was lost — may not be counted toward computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements of Labor Code section 510 or 511. The exception has two built-in ceilings: it does not extend to hours in excess of 11 hours of work in one day, or to hours in excess of 40 hours in one workweek. Each element is stated in the statute: the request originates with the employee; it is in writing; the employer approves it; the lost time results from a personal obligation of the employee; and the makeup hours are worked in the same workweek in which the time was lost.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "If an employer approves a written request of an employee to make up work time that is or would be lost as a result of a personal obligation of the employee, the hours of that makeup work time, if performed in the same workweek in which the work time was lost, may not be counted towards computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements specified in Section 510 or 511, except for hours in excess of 11 hours of work in one day or 40 hours in one workweek."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 513 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 513 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=513.)
  "(Added by Stats. 1999, Ch. 134, Sec. 7. Effective January 1, 2000.)"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 513 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 513 (legislative history note) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=513.)
  Known gap: Section 513 is short and this clause tracks its text closely. The statute does not define "personal obligation," does not itself say whether an employer may decline to approve a request, and does not prescribe a form for the written request beyond the per-occasion signed-request rule quoted in the next clause; the DLSE's published enforcement position on the "personal obligation" element is described in a separate clause below. No published California appellate decision construing the substantive elements of section 513 was located in a CourtListener search for this document — the only published appellate opinion found that discusses the section (Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC (2018) 29 Cal.App.5th 1068, later reviewed by the California Supreme Court on the separate time-rounding and meal-period questions) quoted the statute in a footnote and disposed of the parties' makeup-time dispute as harmless without interpreting the statute, and so is not cited here as authority for its meaning.

A SIGNED WRITTEN REQUEST FOR EACH OCCASION; EMPLOYERS MAY INFORM BUT MAY NOT SOLICIT
Two further rules in Labor Code section 513 govern how the arrangement is initiated. First, the employee must provide a signed written request for each occasion on which the employee asks to make up work time under the section. Second, the statute prohibits an employer from encouraging or otherwise soliciting an employee to request the employer's approval to take personal time off and make up the work hours within the same week. The Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders, which incorporate the same makeup-time provision, add an express statement of what the employer may do: while an employer may inform an employee of this makeup time option, the employer is prohibited from encouraging or otherwise soliciting an employee to request approval to take personal time off and make up the hours within the same workweek.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "An employee shall provide a signed written request for each occasion that the employee makes a request to make up work time pursuant to this section. An employer is prohibited from encouraging or otherwise soliciting an employee to request the employer’s approval to take personal time off and make up the work hours within the same week pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 513 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 513 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=513.)
  "While an employer may inform an employee of this makeup time option, the employer is prohibited from encouraging or otherwise soliciting an employee to request the employer’s approval to take personal time off and make up the work hours within the same workweek pursuant to this subsection."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(M) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(M) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  Known gap: The statute and wage order state the prohibition on encouraging or soliciting requests but do not define those terms or specify the consequence of a violation; this clause does not describe remedies. The wage-order sentence quoted below is from IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(M), which governs professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations; the DLSE Enforcement Manual (quoted in a later clause) states that the IWC incorporated the section 513 language into each of its wage orders except Wage Order 14, but the text of every other numbered wage order was not independently fetched for this document, and the subsection letter and exact wording may differ from order to order.

RECURRING PERSONAL OBLIGATIONS: REQUESTS UP TO FOUR WEEKS IN ADVANCE UNDER THE WAGE ORDERS
The wage-order version of the makeup-time provision contains a sentence that does not appear in Labor Code section 513 itself. Under IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(M), if an employee knows in advance that he or she will be requesting makeup time for a personal obligation that will recur at a fixed time over a succession of weeks — a standing weekly appointment, for example — the employee may request to make up work time for up to four weeks in advance. The same sentence preserves the core same-week rule: the makeup work must still be performed in the same week in which the work time was lost. The wage order otherwise restates section 513's substantive rule in nearly identical terms, including the 11-hour daily and 40-hour weekly ceilings.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "If an employee knows in advance that he/she will be requesting makeup time for a personal obligation that will recur at a fixed time over a succession of weeks, the employee may request to make up work time for up to four (4) weeks in advance; provided, however, that the makeup work must be performed in the same week that the work time was lost."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(M) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(M) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  "If an employer approves a written request of an employee to make up work time that is or would be lost as a result of a personal obligation of the employee, the hours of that makeup work time, if performed in the same workweek in which the work time was lost, may not be counted toward computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements, except for hours in excess of 11 hours of work in one (1) day or 40 hours of work in one (1) workweek."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(M) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(M) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  Known gap: The four-weeks-in-advance sentence is quoted from IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 only; as noted elsewhere in this document, the text of the other numbered wage orders was not independently fetched, though the DLSE Enforcement Manual's own restatement of the wage-order language (quoted in a later clause) includes the same sentence. The "standing weekly appointment" phrase in the body is this document's illustration of the wage order's "recur at a fixed time over a succession of weeks" language, not a quotation. The wage order does not say whether an advance request for a recurring obligation must be renewed after four weeks; the DLSE Enforcement Manual's reading of that point is described in the enforcement-positions clause below.

WHAT "SAME WORKWEEK" MEANS: THE STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF WORKWEEK AND WORKDAY
The makeup-time exception applies only to hours worked in the same workweek in which the time was lost, so the boundaries of the workweek determine whether a given makeup arrangement falls within the exception. Labor Code section 500, which supplies the definitions for the chapter containing sections 510 and 513, defines "workweek" and "week" as any seven consecutive days starting with the same calendar day each week — a fixed and regularly recurring period of 168 hours, seven consecutive 24-hour periods. It defines "workday" and "day" as any consecutive 24-hour period commencing at the same time each calendar day. Under these definitions, a workweek need not run Sunday through Saturday or Monday through Sunday; it is whatever fixed, recurring seven-day period applies to the employee, and lost time made up in the following workweek falls outside the section 513 exception.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(a) “Workday” and “day” mean any consecutive 24-hour period commencing at the same time each calendar day. (b) “Workweek” and “week” mean any seven consecutive days, starting with the same calendar day each week. “Workweek” is a fixed and regularly recurring period of 168 hours, seven consecutive 24-hour periods."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 500 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 500(a)–(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=500.)
  Known gap: Section 500 defines the terms but does not itself say how an employer establishes or changes an employee's workweek, and this document does not address that question. The final sentence of the body draws the straightforward inference from section 513's "same workweek" language combined with section 500's definition; it is not a quotation, and no case law applying the two sections together was located for this document.

THE DLSE'S PUBLISHED ENFORCEMENT POSITIONS ON MAKEUP TIME
The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual addresses makeup time in section 48.2. It states that the IWC incorporated the language of Labor Code section 513 into each of the wage orders except Wage Order 14, and summarizes the elements of the exception as: a written request by the employee to make up time that would be lost due to a personal obligation; makeup hours in one day not exceeding 11 and makeup hours in one workweek not exceeding 40; and, for a recurring personal obligation fixed in time over a succession of weeks, a written request made every four weeks. The Manual notes that the employer is prohibited from soliciting or encouraging employees to request makeup hours, but that informing an employee of the right is permitted. On the undefined "personal obligation" element, the Manual states the Division's enforcement policy: it will not review the reason for the makeup time, so as to allow any employee to determine whether the need to take time off constitutes a personal obligation within the meaning of the statute. A footnote adds that, under AB 1066 (2016) and Labor Code section 861, the makeup-time provisions of section 513 began to apply to agricultural workers covered by Wage Order 14 on January 1, 2017.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "48.2.1 Makeup work exception requires: 1. Written request by the employee to make up time which would be lost by the employee due to a personal obligation 2. Makeup hours worked in one day may not exceed eleven (11) nor, of course, may the number of makeup hours worked in one workweek exceed forty (40). 3. Request may be made for makeup time for a recurring personal obligation which is “fixed in time over a succession of weeks” provided a written request is made every four (4) weeks."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 48.2.1, "Makeup work exception requires" (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 48.2.1 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "The employer is prohibited from soliciting or encouraging employees to make a request for makeup hours, but informing employee of this right is permitted."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 48.2.1.1 (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 48.2.1.1 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "As an enforcement policy DLSE will not review the reason for the make-up time, so as to allow any employee to determine whether the need to take time off constitutes a “personal obligation” within the meaning of the statute."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 48.2.1.2, "Personal Obligation" (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 48.2.1.2 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "The IWC incorporated the language of Labor Code § 513 into each of the orders except 14*:"
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 48.2 and footnote (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 48.2 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "began to apply to agricultural workers covered by Order 14 on January 1, 2017. This includes the “makeup work time” provisions of Labor Code § 513."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 48.2, footnote (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 48.2 n.* (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: The DLSE Enforcement Manual is the agency's own statement of its enforcement policies and interpretations; it is not a statute or regulation and does not bind courts, and California courts have treated positions in the Manual with varying degrees of deference depending on how they were adopted. The Manual's statement that a recurring-obligation request is made "every four (4) weeks" is the agency's reading of the wage order's "up to four (4) weeks in advance" language, not the wage order's own words. The pages quoted carry an "AUGUST, 2019" revision date in their footer; the Manual is revised periodically and later revisions were not checked. Labor Code section 861 and AB 1066 were not independently fetched for this document; the agricultural-worker statement is quoted solely as the Manual's own footnote.

MAKEUP TIME IS NOT "COMPENSATING TIME OFF" UNDER LABOR CODE SECTION 204.3
Makeup time is distinct from "compensating time off" (often called comp time), which is governed by a different statute. Under Labor Code section 204.3, an employee may receive, in lieu of overtime compensation, compensating time off at a rate of not less than one and one-half hours for each hour of employment for which overtime compensation is required by law — that is, overtime hours are actually worked and then banked as paid time off at the overtime rate rather than paid in cash. Section 204.3 conditions that arrangement on a written agreement entered into before the work is performed, a written request by the employee, a regular schedule of at least 40 hours per week, and a 240-hour accrual cap, among other requirements, and it excludes employees covered by several named wage orders. Makeup time under section 513 works differently: no overtime hours are worked at all, because hours shifted within the same workweek (up to 11 in a day and 40 in the week) are simply not counted as daily overtime. The DLSE Enforcement Manual describes section 513 as outlining a makeup work time exception, as opposed to a compensating time off provision, that provides a certain amount of flexibility without compromising the eight-hour-day concept, and it separately cautions that section 204.3 is patterned on a federal provision that applies only to state and local government employees, so that a private employer's use of the state comp-time provisions may result in a violation of federal law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "An employee may receive, in lieu of overtime compensation, compensating time off at a rate of not less than one and one-half hours for each hour of employment for which overtime compensation is required by law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 204.3 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 204.3(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=204.3.)
  "(3) The employee has requested, in writing, compensating time off in lieu of overtime compensation. (4) The employee is regularly scheduled to work no less than 40 hours in a workweek. (c) (1) An employee may not accrue more than 240 hours of compensating time off."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 204.3 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 204.3(b)(3)–(4), (c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=204.3.)
  "Labor Code § 513 Outlines A “Makeup Work Time” Exception, As Opposed to A Compensating Time Off Provision. With the adoption by the Legislature of Labor Code § 513 there now exists a system to provide a certain amount of flexibility without compromising the 8-hour day concept."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 6.3 (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 6.3 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "The provisions of Section 204.3 are patterned on provisions found in 29 U.S.C. § 207(o). It should be noted that these compensatory time provisions are only applicable under the federal law to state and local government employees; the compensating time provisions under federal law are not applicable to employees of private employers."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 6.1.1, "Caveat" (August 2019 revision; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 6.1.1 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause quotes section 204.3's core rule and three of its conditions to draw the contrast with makeup time; it does not restate all of section 204.3's provisions (including its rules on cashing out accrued time, payment at termination, recordkeeping, the wage-order exclusions in subdivision (i), and its inapplicability to overtime-exempt employees). The statement that private-employer use of comp time may violate federal law is quoted as the DLSE's own caveat in Manual section 6.1.1; the federal statute it refers to, 29 U.S.C. § 207(o), was not independently fetched or verified for this document. The DLSE Manual is agency guidance, not binding law.

WHO THE MAKEUP-TIME PROVISION REACHES
Because makeup time operates as an exception to the daily overtime requirements of Labor Code sections 510 and 511, it has practical effect only for employees who are subject to those requirements. Employees who are exempt from overtime — for example, those employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities as those terms are defined in the wage orders — are outside the overtime provisions to begin with; IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 states that the provisions of its sections 3 through 12, which include the section 3(M) makeup-time provision, do not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities. Section 513 also refers to overtime under section 511, which governs alternative workweek schedules, so the exception is written to operate alongside such schedules as well as the standard eight-hour day.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(A) Provisions of Sections 3 through 12 shall not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 1(A) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 1(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  "may not be counted towards computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements specified in Section 510 or 511"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 513 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 513 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=513.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the applicability exception of Wage Order 4-2001 only; each numbered wage order has its own applicability section and its own exemption tests, and those were not independently fetched. The wage-order exemption for administrative, executive, and professional employees depends on duties and salary tests stated in the wage orders and in Labor Code section 515 that this document does not describe. How makeup time interacts in detail with an alternative workweek schedule adopted under section 511 (for example, what the daily-overtime baseline is on such a schedule) is not addressed by the text of section 513 beyond its cross-reference and is not analyzed here.

Employer Representative Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: The makeup-time exception applies only to hours worked in the same workweek in which the time was lost, so the boundaries of the workweek determine whether a given makeup arrangement falls within the exception. Labor Code section 500, which supplies the definitions for the chapter containing sections 510 and 513, defines "workweek" and "week" as any seven consecutive days starting with the same calendar day each week — a fixed and regularly recurring period of 168 hours, seven consecutive 24-hour periods. It defines "workday" and "day" as any consecutive 24-hour period commencing at the same time each calendar day. Under these definitions, a workweek need not run Sunday through Saturday or Monday through Sunday; it is whatever fixed, recurring seven-day period applies to the employee, and lost time made up in the following workweek falls outside the section 513 exception.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 500 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) “Workday” and “day” mean any consecutive 24-hour period commencing at the same time each calendar day. (b) “Workweek” and “week” mean any seven consecutive days, starting with the same calendar day each week. “Workweek” is a fixed and regularly recurring period of 168 hours, seven consecutive 24-hour periods.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 500 defines the terms but does not itself say how an employer establishes or changes an employee's workweek, and this document does not address that question. The final sentence of the body draws the straightforward inference from section 513's "same workweek" language combined with section 500's definition; it is not a quotation, and no case law applying the two sections together was located for this document.

expectedJSON.body: The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual addresses makeup time in section 48.2. It states that the IWC incorporated the language of Labor Code section 513 into each of the wage orders except Wage Order 14, and summarizes the elements of the exception as: a written request by the employee to make up time that would be lost due to a personal obligation; makeup hours in one day not exceeding 11 and makeup hours in one workweek not exceeding 40; and, for a recurring personal obligation fixed in time over a succession of weeks, a written request made every four weeks. The Manual notes that the employer is prohibited from soliciting or encouraging employees to request makeup hours, but that informing an employee of the right is permitted. On the undefined "personal obligation" element, the Manual states the Division's enforcement policy: it will not review the reason for the makeup time, so as to allow any employee to determine whether the need to take time off constitutes a personal obligation within the meaning of the statute. A footnote adds that, under AB 1066 (2016) and Labor Code section 861, the makeup-time provisions of section 513 began to apply to agricultural workers covered by Wage Order 14 on January 1, 2017.

Makeup hours worked in one day may not exceed eleven (11) nor, of course, may the number of makeup hours worked in one workweek exceed forty (40). 3. Request may be made for makeup time for a recurring personal obligation which is “fixed in time over a succession of weeks” provided a written request is made every four (4) weeks.

The Manual's statement that a recurring-obligation request is made "every four (4) weeks" is the agency's reading of the wage order's "up to four (4) weeks in advance" language, not the wage order's own words. The pages quoted carry an "AUGUST, 2019" revision date in their footer; the Manual is revised periodically and later revisions were not checked. expectedJSON.body: Makeup time is distinct from "compensating time off" (often called comp time), which is governed by a different statute. Under Labor Code section 204.3, an employee may receive, in lieu of overtime compensation, compensating time off at a rate of not less than one and one-half hours for each hour of employment for which overtime compensation is required by law — that is, overtime hours are actually worked and then banked as paid time off at the overtime rate rather than paid in cash. Section 204.3 conditions that arrangement on a written agreement entered into before the work is performed, a written request by the employee, a regular schedule of at least 40 hours per week, and a 240-hour accrual cap, among other requirements, and it excludes employees covered by several named wage orders. Makeup time under section 513 works differently: no overtime hours are worked at all, because hours shifted within the same workweek (up to 11 in a day and 40 in the week) are simply not counted as daily overtime. The DLSE Enforcement Manual describes section 513 as outlining a makeup work time exception, as opposed to a compensating time off provision, that provides a certain amount of flexibility without compromising the eight-hour-day concept, and it separately cautions that section 204.3 is patterned on a federal provision that applies only to state and local government employees, so that a private employer's use of the state comp-time provisions may result in a violation of federal law.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 204.3 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An employee may receive, in lieu of overtime compensation, compensating time off at a rate of not less than one and one-half hours for each hour of employment for which overtime compensation is required by law.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 204.3 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (3) The employee has requested, in writing, compensating time off in lieu of overtime compensation. (4) The employee is regularly scheduled to work no less than 40 hours in a workweek. (c) (1) An employee may not accrue more than 240 hours of compensating time off.

citations.quote: Labor Code § 513 Outlines A “Makeup Work Time” Exception, As Opposed to A Compensating Time Off Provision. With the adoption by the Legislature of Labor Code § 513 there now exists a system to provide a certain amount of flexibility without compromising the 8-hour day concept.

citations.quote: The provisions of Section 204.3 are patterned on provisions found in 29 U.S.C. § 207(o). It should be noted that these compensatory time provisions are only applicable under the federal law to state and local government employees; the compensating time provisions under federal law are not applicable to employees of private employers.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes section 204.3's core rule and three of its conditions to draw the contrast with makeup time; it does not restate all of section 204.3's provisions (including its rules on cashing out accrued time, payment at termination, recordkeeping, the wage-order exclusions in subdivision (i), and its inapplicability to overtime-exempt employees). The statement that private-employer use of comp time may violate federal law is quoted as the DLSE's own caveat in Manual section 6.1.1; the federal statute it refers to, 29 U.S.C. § 207(o), was not independently fetched or verified for this document. The DLSE Manual is agency guidance, not binding law.

expectedJSON.body: Because makeup time operates as an exception to the daily overtime requirements of Labor Code sections 510 and 511, it has practical effect only for employees who are subject to those requirements. Employees who are exempt from overtime — for example, those employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities as those terms are defined in the wage orders — are outside the overtime provisions to begin with; IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 states that the provisions of its sections 3 through 12, which include the section 3(M) makeup-time provision, do not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities. Section 513 also refers to overtime under section 511, which governs alternative workweek schedules, so the exception is written to operate alongside such schedules as well as the standard eight-hour day.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 1(A) (California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: (A) Provisions of Sections 3 through 12 shall not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 513 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: may not be counted towards computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements specified in Section 510 or 511

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes the applicability exception of Wage Order 4-2001 only; each numbered wage order has its own applicability section and its own exemption tests, and those were not independently fetched. The wage-order exemption for administrative, executive, and professional employees depends on duties and salary tests stated in the wage orders and in Labor Code section 515 that this document does not describe. How makeup time interacts in detail with an alternative workweek schedule adopted under section 511 (for example, what the daily-overtime baseline is on such a schedule) is not addressed by the text of section 513 beyond its cross-reference and is not analyzed here.
